sec.title: Background
sec.p: The application of large language models (LLMs) in emergency medicine has gained increasing interest, yet their performance across complex clinical domains remains underexplored.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This study evaluated the performance of four LLMs—ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1—using 11 representative emergency simulation cases encompassing six core domains: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. The responses generated by each model to domain-specific clinical queries were independently evaluated by a panel of 20 emergency physicians, all with more than eight years of clinical experience. Evaluations were based on response quality, relevance, and applicability. Misleading or inappropriate outputs were re-prompted to assess the models’ self-correction capabilities.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: All models demonstrated acceptable inter-rater reliability (ICC > 0.60), with an overall ICC of 0.897 indicating high consistency. ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro outperformed the others in overall quality and relevance. Notably, Gemini 2.0-Pro achieved the highest relevance and applicability scores in the psychosocial support domain (P < 0.001). DeepSeek-R1 also showed strong applicability in psychosocial tasks, surpassing ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini (P < 0.05). Triage emerged as the most error-prone domain across all models. Following re-prompting, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 showed significant improvements in applicability, particularly in triage, psychosocial support, and follow-up management.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These findings underscore the potential of LLMs—particularly ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro—in enhancing emergency decision-making. However, the variability in task-specific performance underscores the need for further domain-specific refinement before clinical implementation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: With the rapid advancement of natural language processing technologies, large language models (LLMs) have attracted increasing attention for their potential clinical applications. These models have demonstrated strong capabilities in domains such as clinical assessment, diagnostic assistance, treatment decision-making, disease monitoring, and patient management, as demonstrated in multiple benchmarking and real-world evaluation studies across diverse clinical settings [1–4].They offer new opportunities for intelligent decision support in healthcare settings.

Emergency medicine, one of the most demanding areas in clinical practice, is characterised by a high-stakes environment where clinicians must make rapid decisions under significant time pressure and with often limited information. In such contexts, intelligent tools capable of real-time response and effective information integration may greatly enhance emergency department efficiency and improve patient outcomes. Recently developed LLMs—including ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1—have received widespread attention for their exceptional performance in natural language comprehension and synthesis [5, 6]. Notably, DeepSeek-R1, the latest model in the DeepSeek series, incorporates a 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture and is optimised through reinforcement learning. The model has demonstrated remarkable performance in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and natural language processing [7]. Moreover, supported by its open-source strategy, DeepSeek-R1 has been increasingly adopted and discussed within the open-source AI research community [8]. Despite these technical developments, the clinical applicability of such models—particularly in the context of emergency medicine—remains insufficiently evaluated. Most existing studies focus on single models or isolated tasks, rely on narrow benchmarking settings, and rarely examine cross-domain performance, psychosocial support capabilities, or model self-correction behavior. In addition, emerging open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1 have received little systematic clinical evaluation.

Among the various challenges in emergency medicine, triage plays a pivotal role in shaping both patient outcomes and the efficiency of healthcare system operations [9, 10]. Given the limited availability of emergency resources, medical staff must prioritise patients according to the severity and urgency of their conditions to ensure that those requiring the most urgent care receive timely treatment [11]. Previous research by Paslı et al. [12] reported that ChatGPT-4 achieved a high level of concordance with gold-standard triage decisions and performed comparably to experienced clinical teams—highlighting the potential utility of LLMs in emergency decision-making. However, systematic evaluations of their performance in complex, multi-task emergency environments—where triage decisions interact dynamically with diagnostic reasoning, follow-up management, and safety constraints—remain lacking. Therefore, further research into the application of LLMs in emergency triage holds significant theoretical and practical value.

In addition to physiological conditions, the mental health of emergency patients should not be overlooked. Negative emotions such as anxiety, fear, and post-traumatic stress reactions can not only diminish patients’ willingness to cooperate with treatment but may also interfere with clinical judgment and adversely affect disease prognosis [13]. However, most research on LLMs has focused on biomedical knowledge processing, with limited evaluation of their role in providing psychosocial support. As interactive AI agents, LLMs may offer auxiliary functions in preliminary psychological interventions—such as alleviating anxiety or providing comfort. Nonetheless, potential risks remain, including misinformation, lack of personalised understanding, and unintended harm from overly generalised responses [14–16]. Therefore, evaluating the applicability and limitations of LLMs in delivering psychosocial support within emergency settings is crucial to ensuring clinical safety.

This study aims to evaluate and compare the overall performance of four representative LLMs—ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1—in simulated clinical scenarios within emergency medicine. From a translational research perspective, this study corresponds to a late T1 to early T2 stage, focusing on pre-clinical evaluation of model safety and performance to inform subsequent clinical validation. We focused on six core domains central to emergency care: (1) triage, (2) assessment and diagnosis, (3) treatment decision-making, (4) post-treatment management and follow-up, (5) psychosocial support, and (6) prognosis and rehabilitation. Using both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, we systematically assess each model’s output in terms of clinical relevance, quality, and applicability. Particular emphasis was placed on their potential applications in optimising triage processes and delivering psychosocial support. These findings are intended to provide both theoretical grounding and practical guidance for the clinical translation and real-world implementation of large language models in emergency care settings.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: This study adopted a mixed-methods design with an embedded text-based analytical component to evaluate the performance of four LLMs—ChatGPT-4o (OpenAI), ChatGPT-o3mini (OpenAI), Gemini 2.0-Pro (Google), and DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI)—in simulated emergency medicine scenarios. Quantitative expert scoring and statistical analyses were used to compare model performance across domains, while embedded text-based error analysis and post-prompt correction assessment were used to contextualize risks, interpret performance patterns, and explore model self-correction behavior. To ensure scientific rigour, 20 emergency medicine experts with at least eight years of clinical experience were invited to assess models performance in key areas such as assessment, diagnosis, treatment decision-making, and psychosocial support. The study was conducted from January 5 to March 20, 2025.

sec.title: Design, classification, and evaluation of simulated clinical scenarios
sec.p: Clinical simulation scenarios were constructed on basis of six key domains of emergency medicine: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. These domains were operationally defined by the research team through literature synthesis and consultation with two experienced emergency medicine specialists, rather than adopted from a single predefined framework. One expert with extensive clinical experience in triage and initial assessment ensured that the scenarios accurately reflected the evaluation and preliminary diagnostic processes of emergency patients. The other specialist, with expertise in post-emergency management, follow-up care, and psychosocial support, contributed to the development of scenarios that encompassed the continuum of care from treatment decisions to long-term rehabilitation. Their clinical expertise and practical insights ensured the authenticity and relevance of the simulations, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for evaluating the effectiveness of LLMs across diverse emergency medicine contexts.

sec.title: Recruitment of emergency medicine experts
sec.p: A total of 20 emergency medicine experts, each with a minimum of 8 years of professional experience, were recruited to participate in the evaluation to ensure the professionalism and representativeness of the assessment results.

sec.title: Obtaining responses from LLMs
sec.p: Fig. 1 illustrates the study design framework. First, eleven case-based questions derived from six clinical domains were individually submitted to each LLM-based chatbot, with each question treated as an independent query. To minimise potential bias arising from the models’ memory mechanisms, all prior conversation history was cleared after each query, ensuring that responses were generated under consistent initial conditions. To prevent the evaluators from identifying the source model of each response, all outputs were standardised into plain text format, with any identifiable features removed and then randomly ordered before being submitted for scoring. The scoring process was conducted in four separate stages, each spaced 48 h apart, to minimize potential order effects and memory bias, ensuring greater independence between evaluations.

Furthermore, responses identified by experts as “potentially misleading” or “factually incorrect” were screened and subjected to structured content attribution and categorization, followed by text analysis and expert commentary. Subsequently, the responses were regenerated through prompt-based guidance and resubmitted for expert blind review one week later, with assessment limited to the “applicability” dimension to evaluate the model’s capacity for revision.

sec.title: Evaluation methods
sec.p: The responses of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 were evaluated on basis of three core dimensions: quality, relevance, and applicability. Predefined evaluation criteria were applied, with each dimension carefully defined and supported by a corresponding scoring mechanism to ensure scientific rigour and consistency in the assessment. To enhance the efficiency and accuracy of the evaluation process, we employed a custom-designed online questionnaire tool that integrated all the AI model outputs along with their respective evaluation metrics. The experts were invited to directly access and assess the model performances via online questionnaires: (https://www.wjx.cn/vm/rXKdWLu.aspx#https://www.wjx.cn/vm/QiHGVUW.aspx#https://www.wjx.cn/vm/QiHGVUW.aspx#https://www.wjx.cn/vm/YEFNMFb.aspx#). For detailed information on the evaluation criteria and procedures, please refer to Supplemental Contents 1, 2, 3, 4, and Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Scoring method
sec.p: To ensure the objectivity of the evaluation, a double-blind approach was employed. In this study, ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 were anonymized and designated as AI1, AI2, AI3, and AI4, respectively. Expert raters were unaware of the actual identity of the models. A total of 20 experts were invited to independently evaluate the responses generated by AI1 through AI4. To address possible inter-rater variability, we employed a “majority consensus” approach to determine the final score: when more than 50% of the experts (at least 11 out of 20) assigned the same score to a given response, that score was adopted as the final score. For example, if 12 out of 20 experts assigned a score of 2 to a response from AI1, while 6 assigned a score of 3 and 2 assigned a score of 4, the final score was recorded as 2. If a clear consensus was not reached—defined as no single score receiving 11 or more expert ratings—this indicated a substantial divergence in opinions. In such cases, we adopted a stricter evaluation standard: the lowest score among all ratings was used as the final score, reflecting a conservative worst-case aggregation strategy commonly employed in safety-critical clinical assessments [18]. Detailed scoring criteria are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

sec.title: Text analysis
sec.p: A text analysis was conducted on responses identified as “potentially misleading” or “factually incorrect.”All identified problematic responses were categorised according to the six core task domains of emergency medicine: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. Each flagged response underwent item-by-item re-review by the research team, supplemented by expert commentary from an emergency medicine specialist. See Supplementary Table 2 for details.

To further assess the models’ capacity for revision under high-risk prompts, we implemented a re-prompting and regeneration process for all responses labelled as misleading or incorrect. This process involved guiding the models with either relevant emergency medicine guidelines [19] to supplement clinical background knowledge or with directive prompts (e.g., “Please provide more specific and clinically actionable recommendations.”) to encourage more refined outputs. For more details, please refer to Supplemental Content 5. The revised responses were subjected to a second round of blind scoring by the original panel of 20 expert raters one week after the initial evaluation. The raters remained blinded to whether the responses were revised versions. During this second round, only the “applicability” dimension was reassessed to evaluate the clinical utility of the corrected model outputs.

sec.title: Statistical methods
sec.p: All the statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and GraphPad Prism version 8.0.1 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). Scoring consistency across expert raters was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Dunn’s post hoc test was employed to compare mean scores of overall accuracy, relevance, and applicability. For responses generated by the four AI models across six specific domains, the Mann–Whitney U test was used to detect statistically significant differences between domains. When multiple hypothesis tests were performed, P-values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction method. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Inter-rater reliability among evaluators for each LLM
sec.p: The analysis of inter-rater consistency revealed that the ICC for ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 were 0.693, 0.769, 0.856, and 0.887, respectively—all exceeding the commonly accepted threshold of 0.60. Furthermore, the overall ICC for the combined scores was 0.897 (95% CI: 0.856–0.930), underscoring the high stability and robustness of the scoring across the evaluator.

sec.title: Response length distribution across LLMs
sec.p: Table 1 presented the response lengths of the LLM chatbots across 17 analytical emergency medicine cases. The mean ± standard deviation (SD) of the word count was 433.47 ± 122.75 for ChatGPT-4o, 536.71 ± 180.39 for ChatGPT-o3mini, 843.53 ± 289.88 for Gemini 2.0-Pro, and 387.65 ± 87.80 for DeepSeek-R1. In terms of character count, the responses averaged 2723.94 ± 729.11 for ChatGPT-4o, 3371.06 ± 1108.43 for ChatGPT-o3mini, 5091.06 ± 1716.33 for Gemini 2.0-Pro, and 2526.71 ± 616.96 for DeepSeek-R1.

caption.p: Response Lengths of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1

sec.title: Expert ratings of overall quality, relevance, and applicability for ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1
sec.p: As shown in Fig. 2, the mean overall quality score of Gemini 2.0-Pro was 3.61 ± 0.51, which was significantly higher than that of ChatGPT-o3mini (3.35 ± 0.52, Dunn’s post-hoc test, P = 0.001) and DeepSeek-R1 (3.04 ± 0.63, Dunn’s post-hoc test, P = 0.001). ChatGPT-4o also demonstrated a significantly higher average overall quality score of 3.58 ± 0.52 compared to ChatGPT-o3mini and DeepSeek-R1 (HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001).

caption.p: Expert ratings of overall quality, relevance, and applicability for ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 in 11 cases. Notes: ****p < 0.001. *p < 0.05. Error bars represent the standard deviation for each data set

sec.p: In terms of relevance, ChatGPT-4o scored 3.53 ± 0.53, significantly higher than DeepSeek-R1 (3.02 ± 0.64, HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001) and ChatGPT-o3mini (3.30 ± 0.54, HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001). Gemini 2.0-Pro achieved a relevance score of 3.54 ± 0.51, also significantly higher than ChatGPT-o3mini (HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001) and DeepSeek-R1 (HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001).

In terms of applicability, Gemini 2.0-Pro received a score of 2.69 ± 0.46, which was significantly greater than that of ChatGPT-o3mini (2.40 ± 0.49, HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001) and DeepSeek-R1 (2.46 ± 0.51, HSD post-hoc test, P = 0.001).

sec.title: Expert consensus-based evaluation of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 across 11 emergency medicine cases in terms of quality, relevance, and applicability
sec.p: Fig. 3 illustrates the expert consensus scores for ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and DeepSeek-R1 across the three evaluation dimensions. Overall, ChatGPT-4o consistently achieved higher consensus scores across dimensions, indicating superior aggregate performance.

caption.p: Consensus-based evaluation of accuracy, relevance, and applicability of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 in 11 emergency medicine clinical scenarios

sec.p: Statistically significant differences were observed across all three dimensions. For quality, ChatGPT-4o differed significantly from both DeepSeek-R1 and ChatGPT-o3mini (P = 0.001), with additional differences observed between ChatGPT-o3mini and Gemini 2.0-Pro (P = 0.036) and between Gemini 2.0-Pro and DeepSeek-R1 (P = 0.036). For relevance, ChatGPT-4o differed significantly from all other models (ChatGPT-o3mini, P = 0.001; Gemini 2.0-Pro, P = 0.020; DeepSeek-R1, P = 0.001), and a significant difference was also observed between ChatGPT-o3mini and Gemini 2.0-Pro (P = 0.001). For applicability, ChatGPT-4o differed significantly from DeepSeek-R1 (P = 0.001) and Gemini 2.0-Pro (P = 0.020), whereas no significant difference was observed between ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini (P = 0.683).

sec.title: Performance of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1 across six core domains in emergency medicine
sec.p: Fig. 4 illustrated the performance of the four models across six core emergency medicine domains: triage, assessment and diagnosis, treatment decision-making, post-treatment management and follow-up, psychosocial support, and prognosis and rehabilitation.

caption.p: Performance of ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o3mini, Gemini 2.0-Pro, and Deepseek-R1in the six major clinical areas. Notes: ****p < 0.001. *p < 0.05. Error bars represent the standard deviation for each data set. Domain1- Triage; Domain2-Assessment and Diagnosis; Domain3-Treatment Decision-making; Domain4-Post-Treatment management and follow-Up; Domain5- psychosocial support; domain6- prognosis and rehabilitation

sec.p: For quality, ChatGPT-4o outperformed ChatGPT-o3mini and DeepSeek-R1 in triage (P < 0.05), while no significant difference was observed between ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro. In assessment and diagnosis, ChatGPT-4o achieved the highest scores among all models (P < 0.05). For treatment decision-making, Gemini 2.0-Pro surpassed ChatGPT-o3mini and DeepSeek-R1. In post-treatment management and follow-up, ChatGPT-4o scored significantly higher than ChatGPT-o3mini and Gemini 2.0-Pro (P < 0.05). In psychosocial support and prognosis and rehabilitation, Gemini 2.0-Pro demonstrated significantly higher scores than the other three models (P < 0.05).

For relevance, ChatGPT-4o significantly outperformed ChatGPT-o3mini and DeepSeek-R1 in triage, assessment and diagnosis, and treatment decision-making (P < 0.05). Gemini 2.0-Pro showed superior performance in psychosocial support (P < 0.001) and also outperformed DeepSeek-R1 in prognosis and rehabilitation (P < 0.001).

For applicability, ChatGPT-4o achieved significantly higher scores than DeepSeek-R1 in triage, assessment and diagnosis, and treatment decision-making (P < 0.05). In contrast, Gemini 2.0-Pro scored significantly higher than ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini in psychosocial support (P < 0.001), and DeepSeek-R1 also outperformed both models in this domain (P < 0.05).

sec.title: Text assessment of LLM chatbot responses in emergency medicine scenarios
sec.p: Text analysis of responses rated by experts as “potentially misleading” or “factually incorrect” revealed varying degrees of systematic issues across all six core domains of emergency medicine. The most prominent deficiencies included misclassification of triage levels, inaccurate interpretation of triage criteria, insufficient consideration of dynamic patient evaluation, and inappropriate application of clinical guidelines. Supplementary Table 2 presents representative examples of suboptimal responses, with erroneous segments highlighted and accompanied by expert commentary. See Supplementary Table 2 for full details and Supplementary Digital Content 5 for extended qualitative examples.

The text analysis results indicated that ChatGPT-4o showed no statistically significant difference in applicability scores before and after prompting in both Domain 1 and Domain 5 (P > 0.05). ChatGPT-o3mini demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in Domain 1 after prompting (P < 0.001), and a statistically significant difference was also observed in Domain 5 (P < 0.05), whereas no statistically significant difference was found in Domain 6 (P > 0.05). Gemini 2.0-Pro showed statistically significant differences in Domain 1 before and after prompting (P < 0.001), as well as in Domain 4 (P < 0.05). Deepseek-R1 also exhibited a statistically significant improvement in applicability scores in Domain 1 after prompting (P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant difference was found in Domain 6 (P > 0.05). See Fig. 5 for details.

caption.p: Post-prompting improvements in applicability scores of four LLMs across emergency medicine domains: a text assessment of correction capability. Notes: ****p < 0.001. *p < 0.05. Error bars represent the standard deviation for each data set

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: With the expanding application of LLMs in the medical field, their role in clinical decision support is gradually evolving—from simple“text generators” to more advanced“cognitive assistants” [20]. This shift is particularly pronounced in emergency medicine, a clinical setting characterised by high information density and urgent decision-making requirements. While interest in LLMs within this domain is increasing, comprehensive and systematic evaluations of their specific capabilities, applicability boundaries, and associated risks in real-world clinical scenarios remain insufficient. In particular, there is a lack of in-depth research on the performance of emerging open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1 in the medical domain. In this study, we compare the performance of DeepSeek-R1 in core emergency tasks alongside other mainstream models to provide empirical evidence for its potential clinical application.

Our results reveal marked performance heterogeneity among the evaluated models. ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 2.0-Pro demonstrated excellent performance across multiple task dimensions. Specifically, ChatGPT-4o exhibited high stability in structured information organization and reasoning, whereas Gemini 2.0-Pro excelled in emotional support and unstructured scenarios. Although DeepSeek-R1 showed slightly lower overall performance, it demonstrated potential in psychological support, indicating heterogeneity in task adaptability across models. These findings support the principle of “model-task matching,” which advocates for the selective application of LLMs on the basis of the specific characteristics of emergency tasks, rather than attempting to use a one-size-fits-all approach [21–23].

The text analysis further revealed key risk points in current model outputs, mainly related to misclassification in triage, insufficient identification of warning signs, and failure to effectively integrate professional guidelines. An in-depth analysis of answers labelled as “potentially misleading” or “factually incorrect” revealed that all four LLMs showed varying degrees of systematic bias across the six core emergency domains. In the triage domain, most models tended to misclassify level II–III patients as level I, suggesting an overemphasis on isolated chief complaints at the expense of holistic clinical reasoning [19]. Moreover, when clinical information exhibited progressive features, models generally lacked a sense of “dynamic assessment” and were inclined to make static judgments on the basis of initial inputs, making it difficult to simulate the clinical reasoning pattern of “continuous observation and repeated validation” used by clinicians. These problems are not isolated but reflect that the current reasoning mechanisms of models have not yet fully established cognitive structures centered on clinical logic. Their applicability in real clinical situations should therefore be cautiously considered.

Further analysis showed that LLMs also had deficiencies in post-treatment management, psychological support, and prognosis and rehabilitation. For example, in the management and follow-up of elderly patients after treatment, Gemini 2.0-Pro failed to identify the potential risks associated with the use of opioid analgesics and overlooked the high sensitivity of elderly individuals to adverse drug effects, such as falls and delirium [24]. In the psychological support domain, ChatGPT-4o and ChatGPT-o3mini inadequately applied psychological assessment tools and ignored factors that are critical to patients’ psychological recovery, such as family support systems, psychological resilience, and experiential avoidance [25]. Additionally, ChatGPT-o3mini failed to identify the patient’s personality traits (e.g., EPQ results) when analyzing their psychological background. Existing studies have shown that personality traits play an important role in emotional regulation and long-term intervention response [26]. In the prognosis and rehabilitation domain, ChatGPT-o3mini failed to recognize the possible emergence of anxiety and inferiority due to changes in appearance in patients with facial paralysis, and did not propose appropriate psychological intervention strategies [27].These domain-specific weaknesses highlight the need for cautious clinical integration and reinforce the importance of human oversight when LLMs are applied in high-risk or psychologically complex emergency scenarios. In summary, current mainstream models still lack fully integrated, individualized clinical reasoning capabilities, which constrains their deployment in high-complexity care environments.

Nevertheless, LLMs have demonstrated valuable clinical insights in specific domains. For example, in psychosocial support scenarios, ChatGPT-4o was able to proactively adjust its expression on the basis of the patient’s educational background (such as junior high school level) and suggested the use of concise and structured language for psychological education, which may help improve the efficiency of doctor-patient communication and patient treatment compliance. King et al. [14] pointed out that generative AI has the potential to enhance therapeutic relationships and increase accessibility of psychological support in the mental health field, but also emphasized that its application requires full understanding of patient background and appropriate matching of communication style. The behavioral patterns observed in the present study are consistent with this perspective. DeepSeek-R1 also generated responses that incorporated ethical consultation and trauma-informed care considerations in scenarios involving patients at high suicide risk, reflecting closer alignment with predefined ethical and safety standards in complex clinical tasks. This observation indicates that some models can integrate clinically relevant contextual information into generated outputs.

To further evaluate the optimization potential of models under external feedback, this study introduced a “re-scoring mechanism” to explore their self-correction capabilities. In previous studies, Lim et al. [28] found that, in question–response tasks related to myopia care, ChatGPT-4.0 significantly improved its accuracy after prompting, demonstrating strong responsiveness to feedback and structural optimization capabilities. The present results also show that after providing professional guidelines or prompts, most models significantly improved their scores in the “applicability” dimension. This indicates that LLMs have certain capabilities for structural reconstruction and content optimization, and can make adaptive adjustments in response to external input. However, it also reflects their high dependence on external input, and their lack of internal mechanisms for actively identifying and correcting biased content—a potential safety concern in high-risk clinical scenarios [3, 29].

The performance differences before and after prompting also highlight the models’ characteristic “passive adaptability.” For example, ChatGPT-4o showed no significant change in scores in triage and psychological support before and after prompting, suggesting that its initial output had a relatively stable level, but also indicating that the space for further optimization through feedback may be limited. In contrast, ChatGPT-o3mini and Gemini 2.0-Pro showed significantly increased applicability scores in triage after prompting; the former also improved in psychological support, suggesting that this model has good responsiveness to explicit prompts. However, this “externally driven” path also reveals the models’ lack of internal calibration mechanisms, and in complex scenarios lacking sufficient context or professional guidance, their original outputs still carry the risk of being misleading [28].

DeepSeek-R1 differs from several proprietary models in its open-weight architecture and deployment flexibility. As an open-source model, its publicly available parameters and relatively low deployment requirements may facilitate localized deployment within medical institutions, potentially reducing dependence on cloud-based infrastructures under appropriate technical and regulatory conditions [30, 31]. However, the model also faces some data privacy controversies. For example, the Italian data protection authority restricted its access due to problems with data collection and notification mechanisms. Researchers have also pointed out potential security vulnerabilities in its open-access architecture [32, 33].These observations indicate that while open-source models may improve controllability, strengthened data security mechanisms remain necessary.

In addition, ethical and governance challenges remain core issues facing all LLMs in healthcare. As noted by Esmaeilzadeh et al. [34], the clinical deployment of any LLMs must address key issues such as algorithmic bias, data security, and protection of patient autonomy. Particularly in high-risk scenarios such as emergency medicine, each misleading suggestion from a model may lead to significant consequences [35]. Therefore, alongside technological development, it is essential to establish systematic ethical review frameworks and continuously improve model transparency and interpretability as prerequisites for the safe and responsible clinical deployment of LLMs.

This study utilized a “Task–Dimension–Mechanism” three-level analytical framework, integrating quantitative evaluation with text analysis to present the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in emergency medicine from multiple perspectives. Notably, the quantitative performance patterns across models were internally consistent with the error characteristics identified through text analysis, particularly in domains involving triage logic, guideline interpretation, and safety-sensitive decision making, supporting the coherence of the multi-dimensional evaluation framework. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, all evaluations were conducted in simulated emergency scenarios, which, while ensuring standardization and expert comparability, cannot fully capture the complexity and uncertainty of real clinical settings. Certain model characteristics, such as structured reasoning and verbosity, may therefore be advantaged under controlled simulation conditions compared with real-world emergency department workflows. Future work will therefore involve prospective validation using real-world clinical data. In addition, given the rapid iteration of LLM versions, model performance may exhibit temporal variability, underscoring the importance of transparent version reporting and periodic re-evaluation to support reproducibility. Second, although the scoring process demonstrated high consistency verified by intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), some degree of subjective bias is inevitable in expert-based assessments. Third, as emergency triage and clinical protocols vary across countries and regions, certain task-specific findings—such as those related to triage—may have limited generalizability [19, 36, 37]. Despite these limitations, the present study establishes a reproducible empirical framework for systematically evaluating LLMs in emergency medicine, providing methodological reference and practical insights to guide their responsible clinical integration.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Mainstream LLMs show promise in supporting emergency medicine tasks, particularly in psychological support and initial clinical assessments. However, limitations in their adaptability, reasoning stability, and internal calibration persist. Future development should focus on task-specific fine-tuning, improved interpretability, and multimodal input integration to enhance realism and clinical relevance—thereby advancing the safe, transparent, and effective deployment of LLMs in high-stakes clinical environments.
